id: On the Existence of the Soul

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

How confident I am it is there. Don’t I bring it, As if it were enclosed in a fine leather case, To particular places solely for its own sake? Haven’t I set it down before the variegated canyon And the undeviating bald salt dome? Don’t I feed it on ivory calcium and ruffled Shell bellies, shore boulders, on the sight Of the petrel motionless over the sea, its splayed Feet hanging? Don’t I make sure it apprehends The invisibly fine spray more than once? I have seen that it takes in every detail I can manage concerning the garden wall and its borders. I have listed for it the comings and goings Of one hundred species of insects explicitly described. I have named the chartreuse stripe And the fimbriated antenna, the bulbed thorax And the multiple eye. I have sketched The brilliant wings of the trumpet vine and invented New vocabularies describing the interchanges between rocks And their crevices, between the holly lip And its concept of itself. And if not for its sake, why would I go Out into the night alone and stare deliberately Straight up into 15 billion years ago and more? I have cherished it. I have named it. By my own solicitations I have proof of its presence.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker is deeply confident in the existence and presence of an unnamed inner faculty or consciousness.
- They deliberately expose it to striking natural landscapes, creatures, and sensory experiences for its own enrichment.
- They carefully document intricate details of insects, plants, rocks, and other natural phenomena for it to apprehend.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: How, Don, Haven

outputs.L1:
How confident I am that it is there.  
Don’t I bring it, as if it were enclosed  
in a fine leather case, to particular places  
solely for its own sake? Haven’t I set it down  
before the variegated canyon  
and the undeviating bald salt dome?  

Don’t I feed it on ivory calcium and ruffled  
shell bellies, on shore boulders, on the sight  
of the petrel motionless over the sea,  
its splayed feet hanging? Don’t I make sure  
it apprehends the invisibly fine spray  
more than once?  

I have seen that it takes in every detail  
I can manage concerning the garden wall  
and its borders. I have listed for it  
the comings and goings of one hundred species  
of explicitly described insects.  

I have named the chartreuse stripe  
and the fimbriated antenna, the bulbed thorax  
and the multiple eye. I have sketched  
the brilliant wings of the trumpet vine  
and invented new vocabularies to describe  
the interchanges between rocks  
and their crevices, between the holly lip  
and its concept of itself.  

And if not for its sake, why would I go  
out into the night alone and deliberately stare  
straight up into 15 billion years ago—and more?  

I have cherished it. I have named it.  
Through my own solicitations,  
I have proof of its presence.
outputs.L2:
I have no doubt that it exists. Why else would I carry it with me, like something protected inside an elegant leather container, and take it to certain destinations simply for its benefit? I have placed it before the many-colored canyon and the smooth, unwavering dome of bare salt. I nourish it with ivory-colored calcium, the rippled interiors of shells, coastal stones, and the image of a petrel suspended above the ocean with its spread feet dangling. More than once, I have made certain it perceives the spray too delicate to be seen.

I have watched it absorb every detail I am able to provide about the garden wall and the edges surrounding it. For its sake, I have carefully recorded the movements of a hundred insect species, describing each one precisely. I have identified the yellow-green band, the fringed feeler, the swollen thorax, and the many-faceted eye. I have drawn the trumpet vine’s radiant wings and created fresh language for the exchanges between stones and their cracks, and between the holly’s lip and its own idea of itself.

If I were not doing this for it, what reason would I have to step outside alone at night and intentionally gaze straight upward into a past more than fifteen billion years distant? I have treasured it and given it a name. The very things I have sought out for it prove to me that it is present.
outputs.L3:
The speaker expresses a profound certainty in the existence of an unnamed inner faculty or consciousness—a presence that perceives the world through them and is nourished by what they encounter. To enrich this inward presence, the speaker deliberately seeks out vivid experiences, exposing it to dramatic landscapes, living creatures, and an array of sensory impressions.

This attention to the natural world is careful and exacting. The speaker records the intricate forms of insects, plants, rocks, and other phenomena, dwelling on textures, colors, shapes, and movements so that the inner presence may fully apprehend them. Such close observation does more than preserve external details; it generates new language and encourages imaginative associations between objects, their names, and their deeper identities.

Through this ongoing practice of noticing, describing, naming, and cherishing, the speaker develops a relationship with the consciousness within. Its existence cannot necessarily be demonstrated through conventional evidence, but the speaker regards sustained attention itself as proof. By continually addressing and enriching this presence, they affirm that it is real: something capable of receiving the world, transforming perception into language, and giving meaning to experience.
outputs.L4:
The speaker seeks confidence in the existence of an inner consciousness by guiding it attentively through the natural world. Rather than treating the self as something abstract or separate from experience, the speaker nourishes it with vivid sensory impressions: colors, textures, sounds, movements, and the changing details of the landscape. Each act of observation becomes an act of recognition. By naming what is seen and felt, the speaker gives shape not only to the external world but also to the consciousness perceiving it.

Language is therefore essential to this process. Ordinary words must be stretched, renewed, or expanded so that they can hold the richness of experience. The effort to describe nature reveals the imagination at work, transforming perception into meaning. Attention becomes a form of care, and care becomes a kind of evidence: because the cherished self can notice, name, imagine, and wonder, it can trust in its own reality. Consciousness is affirmed not through logical proof alone, but through its living relationship with the world. In perceiving nature deeply and responding to it with language and awe, the speaker discovers that the named inner self truly exists.
outputs.L5:
### How Don Found Haven

Don had spent years searching for a place where he truly belonged. He traveled through crowded cities, quiet villages, and distant countries, always wondering how he would recognize home when he found it.

One evening, after a long journey, Don arrived in a small coastal town called Haven. The streets were peaceful, the people welcomed him warmly, and the sea seemed to wash away his worries.

That was how Don discovered Haven—not simply as a place on a map, but as a feeling of safety, friendship, and belonging.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical free-verse poem in which the speaker argues for the existence of the soul by describing everything they have shown and taught it.
counterfactuals.output:
I know the soul exists  
because I have taken it everywhere.

I showed it rain  
threading the needles of the pines,  
the small silver industry of ants,  
a train crossing the dusk  
with every window lit  
like a thought refusing sleep.

I taught it the names of losses—  
mother, country, first love,  
the dog waiting years  
inside a single remembered doorway.

I taught it joy, too:  
how strawberries taste of sunlight  
briefly persuaded into flesh,  
how a child’s hand closes around one finger  
and makes a vow  
the mouth cannot pronounce.

I have led it to the sea  
and let the horizon trouble it.  
I have held it before mirrors,  
before graves, before paintings  
where blue was more than blue  
and sorrow wore a gold dress.

At night I showed it the stars,  
those ancient punctures in the dark,  
and taught it how to be astonished  
without demanding an answer.

I taught it shame.  
I taught it mercy.  
I taught it to kneel beside what was broken  
and not ask whether the breaking was deserved.

And if there were no soul,  
what was it that grew quiet  
when the snow began?

What turned within me  
when music entered an empty room  
and found someone there?

What learned, after all these years,  
to love the world  
without believing it would stay?

I cannot point to it.  
Neither can the flame point to heat,  
nor the rose to its red.

But I have shown it everything I could—  
the wound, the wing,  
the bread divided among strangers—

and something in me  
has remembered  
every lesson.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a philosophical prose poem about consciousness as a treasured object carried into nature, using vivid scientific vocabulary, insects, rocks, shorelines, and deep time.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Luminous Specimen**

I carried my consciousness into the wild as if it were a treasured object—a lens wrapped in velvet, a warm geode, a vial of blue fire. I was careful not to drop it among the roots, where beetles worked their black machinery beneath the duff and mycelium threaded the soil with pale synapses.

At the shoreline, tide pools held small republics of anemones, amphipods, and translucent larvae. Barnacles opened their calcareous mouths to the moon’s hydraulics. I set my mind beside them on a slab of basalt, still bearing the dark memory of magma, and wondered whether awareness was substance or aperture: a mineral polished by experience, or merely the gleam that passes over it.

Dragonflies stitched photons above the reeds. Their compound eyes divided noon into thousands of lucid chambers. In the grass, cicadas counted heat with tymbals and nerve ganglia; ants consulted gradients of pheromone, each body a syllable in a sentence no single ant could read. Everywhere, cognition seemed to loosen from the skull and enter the weather.

The rocks kept another counsel. Schist folded under vanished continents. Zircon crystals guarded uranium’s slow confession, atom by atom, through half-lives longer than forests, languages, gods. To hold consciousness against such deep time was to feel its terrible delicacy: this brief electrophysiological jewel, this pulse of ions across membranes, carried for an instant over the Archean dark.

I walked where the surf erased my footprints almost as soon as they were made. Sandpipers probed the shining sediment; trilobites, long absent, seemed to move beneath them in the archive of stone. The sea breathed in orbital rhythms, saline and indifferent, grinding mountains into grains small enough to enter an hourglass.

Still I carried the object. Or it carried me.

By dusk, moths orbited the last ultraviolet rumors among the flowers, and the first stars appeared—fossil light arriving from distances that made solitude feel molecular. I opened my hands. Nothing lay there, yet everything had become more visible: the quartz, the wing case, the foam’s collapsing lattice, the carbon traveling from fern to coal to blood.

Perhaps consciousness is not a treasure because it endures. Perhaps it is treasured because it cannot: a bright, perishable instrument by which the universe, for one coastal moment, touches its own ancient face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary nature poem that begins with “How confident I am it is there” and ends with the speaker claiming proof of an unnamed inner presence.
counterfactuals.output:
How confident I am it is there  
beneath the overpass, where rain  
threads silver through the weeds  
and a fox pauses, bright as a warning.

The river carries our plastic cups  
beside cottonwood leaves,  
making no distinction. Above it,  
clouds refresh their gray pages.

I walk until the city thins  
to wind turbines and thistle,  
until my phone loses its signal  
and the dusk begins uploading stars.

Something keeps pace without footsteps.  
In the dark glass of a pond  
my face loosens into sky;  
a moth taps once against my chest.

I cannot name what answers.

But when the reeds bow, I bow.  
When the hidden frogs begin,  
my blood takes up their rhythm.

This is my proof: it is inside me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of an observant naturalist who catalogs landscapes, shells, birds, insects, and stars as evidence that the human spirit exists.
counterfactuals.output:
**Field Notes on the Invisible**

At dawn I entered the salt marsh  
with a pencil, a glass, and no proof.

I recorded: cordgrass bending east;  
three herons, blue as rain in slate;  
the tide withdrawing its bright ledger  
from the ribs of the shore.

On the beach, shells lay open—  
whelk, moon snail, scallop—  
small abandoned architectures  
spiraled around a vanished tenant.  
I held one to my ear  
and heard not the sea, but longing  
practicing the name of distance.

By noon, the meadow had unfastened  
its cabinets of wings:  
copper butterfly, green darner,  
a beetle lacquered like a dropped star.  
The bees entered foxglove bells  
and emerged furred with gold,  
each carrying, unknowingly,  
the future of a field.

I noted the thrush  
lifting one clear phrase  
through the crowded leaves,  
and the wren, no larger than a fist,  
defending its thorn-house  
with the whole force of music.

At dusk, mountains became  
the dark bones of the earth.  
Above them, constellations appeared—  
the hunter, the swan, the little bear—  
old creatures pinned in fire  
to the immeasurable cloth.

I cataloged what I could:  
mica, feather, carapace, seed;  
the patient geometry of webs;  
the moon’s pale scar;  
a moth asleep in a folded flower.

Yet beside each fact  
another fact remained:

that the eye delights in seeing,  
that the hand grieves to let go,  
that we name what will outlive us  
and love it more for doing so.

Therefore, in the margin, I wrote:  
*Spirit—possible.*

Then crossed out *possible*  
as night opened its black shell  
and all the stars came shining  
from within.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine someone addressing their own soul indirectly. Have them explain, through a series of rhetorical questions and richly detailed images, how carefully they have nourished, educated, named, and cherished it.
counterfactuals.output:
Who was it that fed you, small invisible guest,  
when you came shivering to the door of the ribs?  
Who warmed milk with honey and crushed fennel,  
who held the silver spoon to your silence  
until silence opened like a nestling’s beak?

Who carried you through the long schoolrooms of winter,  
past windows furred with frost, beneath lamps  
whose amber circles trembled on the books?  
Who taught you the alphabet of rain on slate,  
the grammar of roots gripping the dark,  
the difficult arithmetic of loss—  
one chair empty, one coat left hanging,  
one voice subtracted from the evening?

And who gave you your many secret names?  
Did I not call you Ember when grief had nearly quenched you,  
Lark when dawn loosened a song in your throat,  
Harbor when the world came home wounded,  
and Wild Fig when sweetness gathered unseen  
beneath your rough green skin?

Who combed the burrs from your hair after wandering?  
Who washed your feet in a blue basin  
and wrapped them in linen warmed by the stove?  
Who stitched your torn places with threads so fine  
the needle seemed only a glint of moonlight  
passing in and out of cloud?

Was it not I who saved for you  
the ripest pear, the quietest hour,  
the last red coal breathing under ash?  
Who opened the curtains so you might study  
how morning gilds even the cracked cup,  
how dust becomes a galaxy when loved by light?

And when you hid—  
a frightened animal beneath the heart—  
who sat without reaching, without command,  
leaving bread, salt, and a bowl of clear water  
beside the threshold?

Tell me, then, shy tenant of bone and breath:  
have you not been cherished?  
Have I not carried you as a candle through wind,  
one hand cupped around your wavering flame,  
the other feeling its way through the dark?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
